working_title: ASBA and UPI: how your IPO money is held
audience_one_line: A retail applicant who has applied to an IPO through their broker app or bank and wants to understand what actually happens to their money — why it leaves their balance as 'blocked' but isn't debited until allotment, and who the invisible parties (SCSB, sponsor bank, NPCI) are.
must_answer: What ASBA is in plain terms: instead of paying money to the company up front, you authorise your bank to block the application amount in your own account; it stays yours, earning nothing leaving nothing, until allotment is decided.
That ASBA is mandatory for everyone now — retail, HNI, and institutional investors all apply through ASBA.
How UPI fits in for retail: a retail investor applying through an intermediary can use their UPI ID to block the funds; they approve a mandate and the money is blocked, not debited.

Who the hidden parties are and what each does: the SCSB (self-certified syndicate bank that blocks the money), the sponsor bank (the conduit between the exchanges and NPCI that pushes the mandate request), and NPCI (the payments umbrella that runs UPI).
The own-account rule: you must use your own bank account or your own UPI ID; a third-party account gets the application rejected.

What happens after allotment: if you get shares, the money is debited; if you don't, the block is released. The PAN on the application must match the PAN on the bank account or the application is invalid.
must_not_say: Which broker or bank app to use, or any product recommendation.
Step-by-step 'how to apply' instructions beyond what the regulation describes — this explains the mechanism, not a tutorial.
Empirical/market-practice claims ('most people use UPI', 'banks usually block within minutes') not in the source.
Downstream consequences or numbers not present in the excerpts.
The detailed unblocking-deadline mechanics — keep those for the listing-timeline article; here, just that money is released if you don't get an allotment.
angle: Demystify what happens to an IPO applicant's money. Lead with the plain idea — ASBA means your money is blocked in your own account, not paid away — then name the invisible machinery (SCSB, sponsor bank, NPCI, UPI mandate) that makes that possible, grounded in the Master Circular. The reader should finish understanding exactly why their bank balance shows a hold and when it turns into a debit or a release.
notes: Regulation-section article. Single source from cached Master Circular.
